request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis:
The residuals are not noise. The RMS is about 41,870" (roughly 11.6°), the fitted sigma simply absorbed it, and a single 525 d periodogram peak carries power 0.87. So the best model, a power law with n = 2.18, captures the main effect, a prograde apsidal precession of about 38° per orbit, but not the actual shape of the force.

Inferred orbit: the distance range of 1.27–2.07 AU implies a ≈ 1.67 AU and e ≈ 0.24. The Keplerian period for that a would be about 788 d, but the observed period is about 725 d. That points to extra attraction on top of the Sun's Newtonian pull.

Inverse-cube term: the registered Newton-plus-inverse-cube fit sat at eps = 0.01, which is almost certainly its upper bound. For f = -GM/r²(1 + eps/r), the apsidal angle is exactly π/sqrt(1 - eps/p), with p = a(1 - e²) ≈ 1.58 AU. A 38° precession per orbit then requires eps/p ≈ 0.18, so eps ≈ 0.29 AU, far outside the registered bounds. I propose refitting it as a custom law with eps allowed up to 1.5.

Alternatives with one extra parameter: an added linear (Hooke-like) attraction or an added constant attraction. Both also give prograde precession and a shorter period. Comparing them by evidence will help pin down the radial shape.

proposals.rationale: The registered fit hit its bound at eps = 0.01. Matching the exact apsidal angle π/sqrt(1 - eps/p) to the observed 38° per orbit needs eps ≈ 0.29 AU, which would also shorten the period from about 788 d to the observed 725 d.
An extra attraction growing linearly with r is an alternative one-parameter source of prograde precession and a shorter period. It tests a different radial shape from the inverse-cube term.
A constant added radial attraction is the third simple one-parameter shape to compare against the inverse-cube and linear terms.
